newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian gunmen fire on U.S. ambassador's house.
newsitem.headline: Albanian gunmen fire on U.S. ambassador's house.

text.p: Gunmen fired at the U.S. ambassador's residence in Tirana, hitting three cars, and an armed gang forced its way into the Greek consulate in southern Albania to demand visas on Thursday, police said.
Lawlessness which has swept the Balkan country for three months showed no sign of abating despite the impending deployment of a 5,000-strong Italian-led multinational security force.
No one was hurt in the shooting incident at the U.S. residential compound, where Ambassador Marisa Lino lives, police said.
A number of people who work at the embassy live in the sprawling hilltop compound. Lino was at her residence at the time but was unaware of the shooting, an embassy spokesman said.
Police raided homes near the U.S. residential compound, seizing a quantity of weapons and arresting several people. Most foreign diplomats were flown out of Albania last month.
"There were shots last night and three cars of the U.S. embassy were hit. There was no other damage," Colonel Albert Dervishi, who heads Tirana's first police station, said.
"We checked the area. We found arms, ammunition and stolen goods in almost every home," he said. Some people had been charged with the shooting as well as theft and possession of illegal weapons.
The compound is about one km (mile) from the U.S. embassy in central Tirana. For several days youths have tried to storm the U.S. embassy in a desperate attempt to flee their country.
Dozens of police took up positions with assault rifles and bullet-proof jackets on Wednesday and an armoured personnel carrier was parked outside. The area was quiet on Thursday.

In rebel-held Gjirokaster, 30 kms (20 miles) from the Greek border, gunmen with Kalashnikov assault rifles and handgrenades forced their way into the Greek consulate and demanded that 100 passports be stamped with visas.
The gunmen threatened to blow up the building if the visas were not stamped.
People queuing for visas alerted Gjirokaster's rebel-run council. A rebel unit was sent to the consulate and convinced the gunmen to leave without a fight, and without the visas.
It was the fourth time in recent days that the consulate has been attacked: twice by gunshots at night and twice by gunmen forcing their way in.
Albania has been swept by violence since January when a series of fraudulent investment schemes collapsed, wiping the savings of many people.
Rioting over the investment schemes turned into a popular uprising across the country against President Sali Berisha and many regions are now outside of government control.
Rebel "Public Salvation Committees" have been set up to try to run towns such as Vlore, Tepelene, Berat, Korce, Sarande and Gjirokaster. There main demand is that Berisha quit.
The greatest danger now comes from outlaw gangs which have terrorised local populations. The gangs are heavily armed with weapons seized from army depots during the March uprising.
In Athens, visiting Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino secured much-needed support from the European Union and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
EU, OSCE and Greek officials assured Fino, 34, that his all-party crisis government would get organisational, economic and humanitarian aid as well as an Italian-led force to protect relief supplies.

Fino met Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi in Gjirokaster before going to Greece. In Athens he met Prime Minister Costas Simitis, special OSCE envoy for Albania Franz Vranitzky and Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who country holds the rotating EU presidency.

Several EU states have been the driving force behind the multinational force which is due to be deployed in the next two weeks. The OSCE will play a crucial role in monitoring early elections set for June in Albania.
